title: Why Micromanagers Make Bad Teachers
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin critiques the habit of micromanagement, arguing that teachers who hover, over-direct, and constantly intervene in student work and behavior undermine both learning and classroom management. He describes how micromanaging communicates distrust, dampens motivation, and creates anxious, dependent students who look to the teacher rather than developing self-reliance. The piece contrasts micromanagers with teachers who set clear expectations, model thoroughly, and then step back — allowing students to take ownership of their responsibilities. Linsin frames restraint as a skill: knowing when to recede into the background is what allows exceptional teachers to deliver the best outcomes while students rise to meet real independence and responsibility.
points: Micromanaging students — hovering, over-correcting, and constantly intervening — communicates distrust and undermines both motivation and independence.
Excessive movement, tension, and talk from an anxious or overbearing teacher creates nervous energy in students that manifests as poor listening and misbehavior.
Exceptional teachers know when to recede into the background and let students take ownership of tasks and responsibilities they've been taught to handle.
Micromanagement strips the 'heart and soul' out of motivation by interfering with what should be the student's own responsibility.
Teaching students how to speak up for themselves and point out unfairness builds trust and confidence rather than encouraging dishonesty or defiance.
quotes: Excitability is a major cause of misbehavior. And because it’s directly related to the way a teacher carries herself, it’s completely avoidable.
All the movement and tension and excessive talk micromanagers bring with them to the classroom causes nervous energy that manifests itself in poor listening, poor concentration, and misbehavior.

But by knowing when to recede into the background and allow students to do their job, exceptional teachers are able to deliver the best educational experience for their students while receiving the best from their students in return.

For they know that when you micromanage students, when you step in, take on, and interfere with what are their responsibilities . . . You rip the heart and soul out of motivation, suppress real, inspired learning, and unleash a backlash of misbehavior.

Contrary to causing them to be untruthful or argumentative, teaching your students how to square their shoulders and candidly point out injustice engenders loyalty and trust and the confidence to speak up not only for themselves…
